newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-CME aims to recoup lost currency business.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-CME aims to recoup lost currency business.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange will become the first exchange to expose its own capital to market risks when it launches its GLOBEX Foreign Exchange (GFX) facility next month.
The exchange plans to make markets in its own products, in an attempt to recoup currency business lost to the exchange-for-physicals (EFP) market, CME officials said.

GFX will make two-way markets in GLOBEX CME currency futures, hedging GLOBEX trades in the cash market. By doing so, the exchange hopes to make GLOBEX liquid enough and its spreads tight enough to recapture volume lost to EFPs.
GLOBEX is an electronic trading system owned by the CME, Reuters Holdings Plc and the Marche a Terme International de France (MATIF). The CME alone owns GFX.
GFX's board at an October 4 meeting will pick an official start date for the arbitrage unit. CME sources said the exchange has targeted a November 1 launch.

GFX, which received Commodity Futures Trading Commission approval in mid-August, will mark the first time a futures exchange has directly created volume, bankrolled trades and exposed its own capital to cash forex price, trading and delivery risks, CME officials said.

That prospect has some at the CME worried that GFX is not sophisticated enough to avoid, or capitalised enough to withstand, the small trading losses it inevitably will incur, much less any big "hit" from other risks inherent in trading.
"People are going to be waiting, anticipating the startup date, trying to pick them off," a CME source said.
The CME denies that is a legitimate concern.
"No, there's no concern that they're not capitalised enough," said Charles Barwis with CME's GLOBEX marketing.
"There are very strict controls on what can be, in the worst-case scenario, lost in a day," Barwis added.
GFX has set up 106 bank credit lines, and Northern Trust Bank will clear its futures trades, Barwis said.

Some CME members and officials also feared that vital GFX technology and back-office setup might not be solidly in place soon enough and worried that a hasty startup would make CME more vulnerable to GFX's market risks.
"I'm afraid certain people might be hastily bringing this thing to a start, just for the sake of getting it going," the CME source said.

"The trading side has been prepared to go for some time, officially, which gives you an idea of what isn't ready," said another CME source. "You have to have a coordinated back office to go with your front office."
Under GFX, a wholly owned unit of CME, CME will back a team of salaried traders to boost liquidity in GLOBEX electronic after-hours currencies via futures-cash arbitrage.
GFX now has four traders, a chief dealer, an operations manager and a risk manager. It will add a second risk manager and more junior traders.

CME expects GFX bids and offers to better EFP quotes and draw volume -- and open interest -- to GLOBEX. It will compete with some of CME's own member firms and banks in EFP, spot and forward forex, making GLOBEX trades and hedging them in cash.

CME has refused to release budget and capitalisation data or trading strategy plans for GFX, even to its own membership. It said such disclosures would "cause substantial competitive harm," according to a copy of a letter the CME sent the CFTC.
But a CME spokesman last January estimated GFX's costs at $7 million. The second CME source said $5 million of that was capitalisation, with nearly a $2 million annual budget.
Each GFX trader will be allowed to make markets of up to $3 million, about 36 contracts a side, depending on product. GFX will take requests for quotes on 100 lots or larger.

A CME spokesman said GFX will target trading about 3,000 futures contract per GLOBEX session, divided among Japanese yen, German mark, Swiss franc and sterling, with requests for quotes offered in Canadian and Australian dollars.
But some cash forex traders said that amount seemed insignificant, especially spread among four to six currencies.
"There's a lot of cynicism being directed at it," added a trade source familiar with GFX.
Another question is whether GFX can get dealing systems it needs to offset GLOBEX trades efficiently in the cash market.
CME sources said EBS, the electronic foreign exchange brokering service run by a bank consortium, turned down a request by GFX to use its order-matching service.
EBS officials could not be reached for comment.
GFX still is waiting for official word from Reuters Holdings Plc about whether it can use Reuters Dealing 2000-2 system to trade cash forex, the CME sources added.
Those sources said Reuters may not view GFX as a hedger that meets Reuters criteria for Dealing 2000-2.
Reuters officials in London had no comment.
"We're continuing discussions with Reuters and EBS about getting access to those screens," the CME spokesman said.
Dealing 2000-2 is a trade-matching system that requires fewer keystrokes, allows traders to input their own prices and, critically, keeps trading parties anonymous.
Instead, GFX will use Dealing 2000-1, a system that requires punching in more data and taking someone else's price. It also discloses traders' identities.
"With the other system (Dealing 2000-1), everybody will know it's GFX...They're sitting ducks," said the trade source.
Still, some say GFX is better than doing nothing and watching already decimated currency futures flows dry up.

"The EFP market is now so entrenched that it's going to be very difficult to wrest some of that business away," said Leo Melamed, former CME chairman and chairman of Sakura-Dellsher. "But at least it's an attempt in the right direction."
